extracted.intended_audience: small law firms in South Africa; small, medium and micro-enterprises (SMMEs)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical reference guide describing IP rights, South African IP laws and institutions, territorial and international IP principles, and practical measures (registration, portfolio management, commercialisation, enforcement) for small law firms advising SMMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Intellectual Property (IP)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of intangible assets that are the result of ideas, knowledge, creativity, innovation, and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IP covers two broad categories of rights: industrial property, and copyright (including neighbouring rights). The guide presents IP as business assets that can be managed, protected and commercialised to create value for SMMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial property (types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial property covers industry-related IP assets of economic importance. The main types of industrial property include trade marks, patents and designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade marks: used to distinguish goods or services; Patents: for inventions; Designs: related to the appearance (aesthetic design) or function (functional designs) of industrial products. Each type is treated as a distinct statutory right with its own protection/registration regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and neighbouring rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects original works, focused primarily on the creative industries; neighbouring rights protect people who are not the creators (e.g., performing artists, producers, broadcasters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of protected subject-matter include artistic and literary works, recordings, photographs, advertising materials and website content. Related statutes and regulations (e.g., Copyright Act, Regulations, proposed amendments) govern registration and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) as legal protections
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs are legal protections that give the creator ownership of the IP, providing exclusive rights of use and the right to earn recognition or gain financial benefit, usually for a limited period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPRs confer time-limited exclusivity and economic exploitation rights; these protections are implemented through statutory regimes and/or recognised at common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rights vs common law rights
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs can come into being through both statute and common law: statutory rights are established by Acts (e.g., trade marks, patents, designs), while common law rights are derived from legal precedents and apply where legislation does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a business does not register a trade mark, it can rely on common law actions such as unlawful competition or passing off. Common law remedies operate alongside statutory rights and are continuously developed by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-relationship and overlap of IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although each IPR subsists and is enforced separately, a single product or creation can contain several underlying rights, which overlap with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide uses the 'Kreepy Krauly' case study to show how one product may simultaneously involve trade marks (name), copyright (drawings/manuals/packaging), patents (invention), designs (aesthetic/functional features), trade secrets (manufacturing/process data) and common law goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secrets (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secrets cover technical information, manufacturing process, research data and commercial information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secrets are protected by secrecy measures rather than registration; they should be 'closely guarded' and managed via contracts, access controls and business practices to preserve protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade marks (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade marks include words, names, letters, numerals, logos, colours, shape configuration used to distinguish goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade marks should be registered where possible; if unregistered, common law remedies may still apply. Trade mark practice and regulations (Trade Marks Act, Regulations) govern filing and enforcement in South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright (examples of protected materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects logo design, drawings, instruction manuals, photographs, advertising material, website content & layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright protection arises automatically but statutory regimes (Copyright Act, Regulations, Amendment Bill) determine specific rights and enforcement options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents protect inventions and methods for improvements & innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent protection is territorial and statutory (Patents Act and Regulations). The PCT provides a unified procedure to file patent applications across contracting states; PCT effective in South Africa from 16 March 1999. Specific patentability criteria and procedures are governed by statute and CIPC practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs cover aesthetic and functional features of products, parts & fittings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs may be registered under the Designs Act and subject to Designs Regulations. Functional vs aesthetic distinctions matter for eligibility and registration strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of territoriality of IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs are limited to the territory where they have been granted; a state has authority over acts that take place within its own territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IPR registered in South Africa does not automatically give rights beyond the border — protection must be sought in each territory where the IPR is used in trade. International treaties set minimum standards and enable cross-border strategies (e.g., PCT, Paris, Berne, TRIPS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant international treaties and mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is a member of international IP treaties including the Paris Convention, Berne Convention, Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT), and TRIPS Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These treaties establish filing priorities, unified procedures (PCT), minimum standards (TRIPS) and cross-border recognition frameworks. The guide notes anticipated accession to Hague and Madrid Protocols in the future and that CIPC administers many treaties on behalf of South Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of international organisations in IP
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO, WTO, WCO and INTERPOL play roles in protection, enforcement and international cooperation on IP issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO administers major treaties and provides cross-border services; WTO administers TRIPS; WCO assists with customs enforcement for counterfeits; INTERPOL helps police combat international IP crime (counterfeiting, piracy, cybercrimes). Links to organisation portals are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: South African IP legal system characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa has a mixed legal system (Roman Dutch, English common law, Indigenous/customary law) and is a constitutional state; international agreements become law when enacted nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common law is modified by statutes and interpreted by Superior Courts. Practitioners must consider constitutional consistency and statutory frameworks when advising clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key South African IP statutes (must consult)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important statutes include: Trade Marks Act 194 of 1993; Designs Act 195 of 1993; Patents Act 57 of 1978; Copyright Act 98 of 1978; Registration of Cinematograph Films Act 62 of 1977; Performers Protection Act 11 of 1967; Plant Breeders’ Rights Act 15 of 1976; Counterfeit Goods Act 37 of 1997; National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004; Merchandise Marks Act 17 of 1941 (and amendments); Agricultural Products Standards Act 119 of 1990; Intellectual Property Rights from Publicly Financed R&D Act 51 of 2008.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide lists legislation and links; practitioners should review current statutes and regulations when advising clients as law and practice change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC) functions
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPC's functions include registration of companies and co‑operatives; IP protection via registration/maintenance/safeguarding of trade marks, copyright, designs and patents; public disclosure through business registers; compliance monitoring; education and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CIPC IPOnline is the official portal for IPR services in South Africa — users must register as CIPC customers and create IPOnline profiles to use the system. The CIPC website provides practice notes, legislation and related links useful for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use common law remedies (practical tip)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a business does not register its trade mark, it can use common law actions such as unlawful competition or passing off to act against unauthorised use of the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common law remedies provide alternative enforcement routes but are fact-specific and developed by courts; practitioners should weigh costs and evidentiary requirements when advising SMMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical aims for small firms advising SMMEs
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide aims to equip small law firms to advise clients on protecting IP assets; connect SMMEs to government/business support organisations; and facilitate access to funding for IP protection and commercialisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide offers: overview of IP value chain (registration, portfolio management, commercialisation), guidance on protecting IP globally, practical advice on IP valuation and negotiation skills, and information on support structures and funding opportunities. It emphasises viewing IP as a strategic business tool rather than merely an administrative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case studies to illustrate IPR interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the Kreepy Krauly case study to demonstrate how different types of IPRs intersect in a single product (trade mark, copyright, patent, designs, trade secrets, common law goodwill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies are presented as practical illustrations to help practitioners recognise multiple overlapping rights in real products and plan combined protection and enforcement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and resource consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidated lists of resources, links to government departments, IP organisations, and the main IP laws/regulations/treaties are provided for practitioner reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide contains Part 5: resources including glossary, CIPC resources, general resources and full lists of main IP laws, regulations & treaties with links — recommended as a practical toolkit for advising clients and for up-to-date legal research.
